results.question: According to “A new clump-based star formation model for galaxy simulations: implications for high-redshift compact star clusters”, how does increasing disc compactness (ξ) from 0 to 10 in 10^10 M☉ haloes affect (a) the maximum gas clump mass and surface density, (b) the fraction of clumps exceeding a surface density threshold Σc,th = 300 M☉ pc^-2, and (c) the global star formation efficiency at t = 3 t_dyn? Please answer with the quantitative values reported in the paper.
results.reference_answer:
(a) Maximum clump mass increases from ≈ 10^5.1 M☉ at ξ = 0 to ≈ 10^7.4 M☉ at ξ = 10; maximum clump surface density increases from ≈ 10^2.9 M☉ pc^-2 to > 10^4.0 M☉ pc^-2. (evidence_id: 0c3dbf13da9dd4027969933c)

(b) The fraction of clumps with Σc ≥ 300 M☉ pc^-2 rises from 0.25 at ξ = 0 to 0.34 at ξ = 6 and 0.38 at ξ = 10. (evidence_id: 0c3dbf13da9dd4027969933c)

(c) The global star formation efficiency at t = 3 t_dyn increases monotonically from 5 × 10^-3 at ξ = 0 to 2 × 10^-1 at ξ = 10 (for the 10^10 M☉ haloes). (evidence_id: 160dd9270d4a618cf6df643a)

We have investigated how the compactness of galactic discs regulates clumpy star formation and the formation of bound star clusters. To this end, we have developed a new star formation model (CSF) in which star-forming gas clumps are identified on-the-fly and converted into stars with an efficiency _𝜖_ SF set by the clump surface density Σc, calibrated against the radiation hydrodynamics simulations of Fukushima & Yajima (2021). We apply the model to isolated disc galaxies embedded in haloes of _𝑀_ h = 10[9] , 10[10] and 10[11] M⊙ with a fixed gas-to-halo mass ratio of 0 _._ 01, adopting disc scale radii 

appropriate for _𝑧_ = 0–10 as a proxy for compactness. Our main results are summarised as follows. 

(i) Compact discs form more massive and denser gas clumps. In the 10[10] M⊙ haloes, the maximum clump mass increases from ∼ 10[5] _[.]_[1] to 10[7] _[.]_[4] M⊙ and the maximum clump surface density from ∼ 10[2] _[.]_[9] to _>_ 10[4] _[.]_[0] M⊙ pc[−][2] between _𝑧_ = 0 and 10. The fraction of clumps exceeding Σc _,_ th = 300 M⊙ pc[−][2] rises from 0 _._ 25 at _𝑧_ = 0 to 0 _._ 34 at _𝑧_ = 6 and 0 _._ 38 at _𝑧_ = 10, and the most compact discs host clumps with _𝜖_ SF ∼ 1.

The maximum clump mass increases surface density of 300 M⊙⊙ pc[[−][2]][[2]] rises from 0 _._ 25 to 0 _._ 38 10[[10]] M⊙⊙ haloes and from 2 × 10 × 10 10[[−][2]][[2]] to 4 × 10 × 10 10[[−][1]][[1]] in 10[[11]] M⊙⊙ feedback disrupts the gas discs of the most compact systems, cluster mass fraction reaches ≈ ≈ 40 per cent at _𝑧_ ≥ 8 and ≈ ≈ broadly consistent with those inferred for high- _𝑧_ **Key words: 1 INTRODUCTION** How galaxies convert gas into stars on the scale of individual clouds remains one of the central unsolved problems in galaxy formation. Stars form within giant molecular clouds (GMCs), which are clumpy and dense structures embedded in the interstellar medium (ISM), and the efficiency of this conversion is regulated by the interplay between self-gravity and stellar feedback. Once massive stars are born, stellar feedback processes such as photoionisation, radiation pressure, and supernova (SN) explosions inject energy, momentum, and metals into the surrounding ISM, dispersing their parent GMCs (e.g. Kruijssen et al. 2019; Chevance et al. 2022; Schinnerer & Leroy 2024; Härer et al. 2025; Wainer et al. 2026). The dispersed gas subsequently cools, re-condenses, and forms new GMCs, where the next generation of stars emerges (e.g. Inutsuka et al. 2015). This continuous gas–star cycle regulates the evolution of galaxies from the early Universe to the present day. Understanding how gas within GMCs is converted into stars is therefore essential for revealing the physical mechanisms that drive galaxy formation and evolution.

We emphasise that these simulations are idealised since the discs are isolated and non-cosmological, the halo-to-disc mass ratio is fixed, and no stellar disc is included in the initial conditions. Thus, environmental effects, gas accretion, and hierarchical growth are absent by construction. The controlled setup adopted here allows the effects of compactness to be isolated, and the next step is to test the same physics in a cosmological context, where disc sizes, gas accretion and merger histories are set self-consistently rather than as free parameters. ## **2.1 Star Cluster Formation Simulations** 

In this work, we use the Turbulent Clump Core Accretion (TCCA) star cluster formation models developed by Farias et al. (2017, 2019); Farias & Tan (2023), where star clusters are formed inside magnetized, turbulent, gravitationally bound, and initially starless clumps within giant molecular clouds (GMCs). These consist of a suite of unique _𝑁_ -body simulations focused on accurately following stellar dynamics in the early stages of star cluster formation, i.e., where there is still ongoing formation of stars. These models assume individual stars and primordial binary stars form via stochastic core accretion with initial clump properties based on the Turbulent Core Accretion (TCA) model (McKee & Tan 2003). Farias et al. (2017) (hereafter, Paper I) presented the extreme case of instantaneous star cluster formation, where all stars are formed together at once and remaining gas is assumed to leave the system instantaneously according to a given global star formation efficiency (SFE, _𝜖_ ). Farias et al. (2019) and Farias & Tan (2023) (hereafter, Papers II and III, respectively) presented the case of gradual star cluster formation. In these simulations, we assume that a fraction ( _𝜖_ ) of the gas is gradually converted into stars while the remaining gas is also steadily removed from the system due to stellar feedback. This is modeled as a linear decrease of the gas reservoir (Equation 9, Paper III) until it reaches zero at the end of star formation, _𝑡★_ . The timescale over which this process occurs is set by the star formation efficiency per free-fall time, _𝜖_ ff, such that higher values of _𝜖_ ff result in shorter _𝑡★_ (see Paper III for details). The case of _𝜖_ ff = ∞ corresponds to the instantaneous case where all stars are formed at once, whereas the slowest case considered assumes _𝜖_ ff = 0.01. For this paper, we post-processed clusters formed from _𝑁_ -body models outlined in Paper III.
